item.title: Bridging digitalisation, sustainability, and resilience through systems thinking tools: Integrated perspectives and collaborative practices for SMEs
item.content:encoded:
Rui Torres de Oliveira, Deakin University

Agnes Toth-Peter, University of Queensland

Martie-Louise Verreynne, University of Queensland

David Audretsch, Indiana University

Domenico Dentoni, MBS School of Business

Andrea Chiarini, University of Verona

The 21st century presents a range of complex and interdependent challenges, including climate change, resource depletion, economic inequality, and technological disruptions. These so-called wicked problems demand a paradigm shift in our approach to problem-solving. Addressing such challenges requires multi-stakeholder partnerships and holistic, systems-level approaches that transcend traditional, siloed methodologies. Systems thinking, a powerful tool for understanding complexity and interconnections, offers a pathway to sustainable solutions.

Appel publié par Journal of Small Business Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Applications of systems thinking tools, such as causal loop diagrams (CLDs), system archetypes, and system dynamics modeling, in addressing sustainability challenges
  • Development and validation of systems-level frameworks and methodologies for sustainable development
  • Case studies demonstrating the impact of systems thinking on real-world sustainability and/or digitalisation initiatives
  • Use of group model building and participatory system dynamics to support interdisciplinary and ecosystem solutions
  • Exploration of system archetypes and system dynamics models to identify leverage points for driving transformational change and to investigate levers in cross-boundary settings
  • The role of digital technologies, including IoT, AI, big data, and blockchain, in enabling systems-level insights and solutions in the circular economy and sustainability initiatives
  • Integration of digitalisation with circular economy strategies and Industry 5.0 principles and potentials
  • Innovative approaches to digital transformation that promote sustainable development
  • Cross-sectoral and interdisciplinary research to foster collaboration in bridging sustainability and digitalisation, using systems thinking
  • The role of ecosystems in sustainable business models and the boundaries of entrepreneurial ecosystems
  • Methodologies for recognising, assessing and addressing the interconnectedness of environmental, economic, and social systems
  • Open innovation in new sustainable businesses, considering distinct institutional contexts and economic systems, such as emerging and developed economies

Timeline

  • October 1, 2026: Rolling submissions begin
  • May 31, 2027: Manuscript deadline for rolling submissions

item.title: Organizing Sustainably with Nature in the Global South
item.content:encoded:
Simone Barakat, Fundação Getulio Vargas

Maria Ehrnström-Fuentes, Hanken School of Economics

Seray Ergene, University of Rhode Island

Steffen Farny, Leuphana University Luneburg

Judy Muthuri, University of the West Indies

Contemporary sustainability challenges increasingly foreground organizations as embedded within complex social-ecological systems rather than operating independently from them. While ecological degradation and resource constraints affect organizations worldwide, these challenges are more immediate and structurally embedded in the operating environments of the Global South. These challenges are not just a background context to which organizations must adapt but an outcome of long-standing patterns of extraction, uneven development, and entrenched social inequalities that continue to shape what sustainability can mean in practice.

Appel publié par Organization & Environment. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Organizing for Environmental Sustainability across Communities and Regions - How do communities and organizations work together to govern natural resources and shared ecological commons?
  • How do sustainability standards, certifications, and supply-chain rules influence organizational practices across regions?
  • How do organizations manage environmental interdependencies across local and global contexts?
  • What challenges arise when local ecological priorities clash with global market or regulatory pressures, and how do organizations deal with these challenges in practice?
  • Organizing with Nature from a Global South perspective - How do organizations in the Global South manage their activities within the carrying ecological capacity of the planet (i.e., planetary boundaries), particularly under conditions of resource constraints and institutional fragility?
  • How do organizations in the Global South engage with degrowth, sufficiency, circular, or regenerative practices?
  • What tensions do organizations in the Global South face between economic survival and ecological realities, and how do they navigate these circumstances in practice?
  • How organizations in the Global South conceptualize and manage their embeddedness within social–ecological systems and attempt to develop a regenerative dynamic with nature?
  • Power, Inequality, and the Governance of Nature - What are the sources of environmental injustices currently in the global South? How are they experienced? What are some resistances to these injustices, and how do they unfold? What are some policy mechanisms (if any) to address these injustices?
  • How do power asymmetries manifest in sustainability governance and transnational regulations?
  • How do corporations influence environmental policy and access to natural resources?
  • How do resistance and counter-organizing emerge around contested environmental futures?
  • Stakeholders and Environmental Sustainability from a Global South Perspective - How do organizations in the Global South engage with stakeholders in relation to environmental sustainability?
  • How are the interests of diverse stakeholders, such as communities, governments, NGOs, and other stakeholders, navigated around environmental risks and resource use?
  • How do stakeholder relationships influence organizational decisions and practices related to environmental sustainability?
  • How do power asymmetries and dependency relations among stakeholders shape environmental outcomes and organizing processes?

Timeline

  • October 20, 2026: Paper Development Workshop
  • February 28, 2027: Full manuscript submission deadline

item.title: Collective actorhood and organizationality: Recalibrating responsibility in business-society relations
item.content:encoded:
Dennis Schoeneborn, Copenhagen Business School

Héloïse Berkowitz, CNRS, Aix Marseille University

Leonhard Dobusch, University of Innsbruck

Frank de Bakker, IÉSEG School of Management

Consuelo Vásquez, Université du Québec à Montréal (UQAM)

Over the past decades, the relations between business and society have fundamentally changed. We are entering an age of digital futures with artificial intelligence taking over more and more human tasks at rapid speed, as well as broken futures with accelerating dynamics of climate change, in which the survival of humankind will depend on our ability to organize in collective ways and imagine alternatives to tackle such complex social problems, amidst growing inequalities and ecological destruction on a planetary scale.

Appel publié par Business & Society. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How is collective actorhood performed and organized?
  • Is a legal status/legal person needed to accomplish collective actorhood?
  • Why and how do actors strategically downplay or amplify collective actorhood? How do these strategic efforts affect responsibility attributions?
  • What are the implications and limitations of collective actorhood for reenvisioning the business-society relationship and offer alternative solutions in crises of civilization?
  • Where and how does actorhood emerge? How do institutional contexts affect actorhood?
  • How does actorhood evolve over time or space, and how do organizations transition between different degrees of organizationality?
  • Can social collectives be perpetuated and maintained even with a low degree of organizationality – or do they feel pressures either to be dissolved or evolve toward higher degrees of organizationality eventually?
  • How to explain asymmetric dynamics between the organized (e.g., established formal organizations; high degree of organizationality) and the (rather) unorganized as their counterparts (e.g., social media firestorm; low degree of organizationality)?
  • What can we learn from alternative forms of organizing, including those in marginalized settings?
  • How is collective actorhood conceptualized in the various geographies, including the Global South? How does this translate, circulate, and adapt across geographies?
  • What are the contributions of other collective notions stemming from indigenous cosmovisions and decolonial approaches?
  • How does actorhood affect the interactions between organizations from different domains (for profit and non-profit, scientific organizations, public actors, etc.)?
  • When does collective actorhood create relations of domination and exploitation?
  • At what point does collective actorhood become constitutive of societal problems and crises (incl. fascism, techno-feudalism, etc.) – rather than a solution for addressing them?
  • How does actorhood (or the lack of) affect the relationship between privileged and marginal communities?
  • Can living (forests, rivers, soils) and non-living (algorithms, technologies) entities be attributed actorhood and be held accountable? How does it differ from 'human' organizing?
  • How can alternative ontologies help inform this analysis?
  • How can a gradual understanding of organization help us to understand variations in the degree of organizational actorhood and responsibility attributions in the relations between businesses and society?
  • What are the parameters of organizationality required for a responsible collective actorhood?
  • How can alternative ontologies, cosmovisions, and organizing experiences inform this critical reflection?
  • How to better account for situations in which marginalized actors are forced into fluid and precarious ways of organizing and/or have no choice to lessen the degree of organizationality to cope or survive?

item.title: Organizing within the Planetary Boundaries
item.content:encoded:
Steve Kennedy, Rotterdam School of Management, Erasmus University

Brooke Lahneman, Montana State University

Lucrezia Nava, University of Exeter Business School

Amanda Williams, EM Lyon Business School

Scholarship on business sustainability increasingly views organizations as embedded within natural systems, conceptualized through the planetary boundaries framework. The planetary boundary framework defines nine Earth system processes that regulate the planet's stability and resilience and are directly affected by human activity. Alarmingly, seven of these nine boundaries have now been crossed, threatening both natural systems and the economies that depend on them. For business scholarship, this creates an urgent need to understand how organizations can operate and manage within the safe space delineated by planetary boundaries.

Appel publié par Organization & Environment. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How Organizations Integrate the Planetary Boundary Framework into Strategy and Action
  • How organizations leverage planetary boundaries to inform sustainability materiality assessments and sustainability strategies
  • How organizations collectively use planetary boundaries as a basis to inform shared understanding of cross-scale risks across space and time
  • How organizations leverage planetary boundaries to inform risk management approaches
  • How organizations collectively build adaptive capacity for addressing risks and identifying opportunities associated with the planetary boundary framework
  • How organizations utilize planetary boundaries to inform creation of sustainability targets such as SBTi and corporate reporting on environmental impacts
  • How organizations disaggregate planetary boundaries to relevant temporal and spatial scales to inform appropriate action for sustainability
  • How organizations use the planetary boundary framework to shape sectoral and cross-sector collaborations
  • How organizations leverage planetary boundaries as a way to 'unlock' the complexity of the natural environment for business model innovation and/or product design
  • How Organizations Can Operate and Manage within Individual Planetary Boundaries
  • How organizations detect, interpret, and act when a planetary boundary is being approached or transgressed
  • How organizations prepare for risks associated with transgressing the boundaries and innovate to limit planetary boundary transgression
  • How organizations use planetary boundaries for constraint-driven innovation for enhanced practices, processes, business models, and/or collaborations
  • Which processes and practices enable firms to develop proactive and responsive strategies for long-term engagement with a specific planetary boundary
  • How organizations should balance trade-offs between proactive and responsive strategies for a given planetary boundary, given their industry and operating context
  • What roles different stakeholders play in shaping organizational responses to planetary boundary transgressions
  • How organizations can engage with least-studied boundaries such as ocean acidification, biogeochemical flows, atmospheric aerosol loading, stratospheric ozone depletion, and novel entities
  • How to Navigate Interconnections among Planetary Boundaries and with Social Foundations
  • How organizations adapt and innovate strategies, practices, and processes to address interconnections among multiple planetary boundaries
  • How efforts to stay within planetary boundaries can be aligned with advancing key social foundations and UN Sustainable Development Goals
  • How organizations can apply systems-thinking lenses to manage non-linear change, ecosystem risks, and feedback loops across planetary boundaries and/or social systems
  • What governance mechanisms, decision tools, or collaborative arrangements enable organizations and industries to navigate and manage trade-offs across boundaries
  • What role could concepts such as degrowth, carrying capacity, or post-growth business models play in helping organizations remain within interconnected ecological limits
  • How to Develop Alternative Organizational Theories and Practices from Planetary Boundary Biophysical Foundations
  • What innovations in practices, products, and business models emerge when organizational thinking begins with planetary boundaries
  • How integrating the planetary boundary framework can inform or reshape core organizational theories
  • How the planetary boundary framework can inform theory on crisis management and responding to ecosystem shocks such as natural disasters
  • How the planetary boundary framework might advance perspectives on desirable or alternative futures
  • What alternative forms of organizing can be theorized by taking planetary boundaries as foundational
  • How theory on circular and regenerative systems can be informed by considering planetary boundaries

Timeline

  • March 1, 2027: Full manuscript submission deadline

  • Gail Whiteman, University of Exeter Business School

item.title: Reimagining Accounting for Inclusive Capitalism
item.content:encoded:
Charl de Villiers, University of Auckland

Ruth Dimes, The Open University

Anwar Halari, The Open University

Matteo Molinari, University of Bergamo

Capitalism remains the dominant framework for organising global economic life, yet its promises of prosperity and inclusion have increasingly come under scrutiny. Over the past few decades, the richest 1% have captured more than half of global wealth, while environmental degradation has accelerated at an alarming rate, threatening planetary boundaries. These outcomes have prompted growing calls for more inclusive and sustainable forms of capitalism, leading to the emergence of the concept of Inclusive Capitalism. Inclusive Capitalism seeks to reconcile profit-making with broader societal goals such as environmental stewardship, social justice and economic inclusion. However, its very emergence implies a failure of traditional neoliberal capitalism to deliver on its promises of inclusivity and prosperity. The push for Inclusive Capitalism thus reflects a growing recognition of capitalism's contradictions and the need to rethink how value is defined, measured and distributed.

Appel publié par Accounting, Auditing & Accountability Journal. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Historical and Conceptual Foundations: How has capitalism been historically conceptualised and what role has accounting played in shaping the boundaries of inclusion and exclusion in capitalist systems?
  • Accounting and the Language of Inclusion: How is capitalism linguistically constructed in corporate reports, policy documents, and the media? Why and how has the term 'capital' become associated more with financial capital than other forms of capital (natural, social, human, intellectual) and what are the implications of this? How do metaphors and anthropomorphic representations influence perceptions of accounting's role?
  • Accounting and Technology: How are emerging technologies shaping accounting practices that either widen or narrow inclusion? How might they entrench exclusion, concentrate power, or reinforce surveillance logics within capitalist systems? How is capitalism represented and contested in digital platforms and social media?
  • Critical Perspectives: How do accounting practices reflect and reproduce capitalist logics? What are the tensions between accountability, transparency, and inclusion in capitalist enterprises? Can alternative frameworks (e.g., feminist, indigenous, or social accounting) challenge dominant paradigms?
  • Institutional and Policy Dimensions: How can governments, regulators, and standard-setters use accounting to promote more inclusive and responsible capitalism? What are the implications of developments such as integrated reporting, sustainability standards, and ESG metrics?
  • Religion, Culture and Norms: How do religious organisations, cultural traditions and societal norms shape accounting practices and in what way do these practices create pathways that can support financial and social inclusion, or, conversely, undermine such goals?
  • Management Accounting Practices: How can management accounting systems incorporate multi-capital perspectives? What role do incentive structures and performance measurement play? How do managers change the way they think and act to reflect more integrated and inclusive ways of thinking about value creation?

Timeline

  • June 5, 2026: Notification of Acceptance for Workshop
  • July 7, 2026: Workshop date in Bergamo, Italy
  • November 1, 2026: Opening date for manuscripts submissions
  • January 31, 2027: Closing date for manuscripts submission

item.title: Building Digital Capabilities for Improved ESG Performance of Entrepreneurial Firms: Strategies for Tackling Challenges and Capitalizing on Opportunities
item.content:encoded:
Stefano Bresciani, University of Torino

Jawad Abbas, James Cook University

Fauzia Jabeen, Abu Dhabi University

Technological advancements require entrepreneurial firms to strategically develop digital capabilities to enhance their competitiveness, innovation capacity, and sustainable performance. This collection seeks to explore how such firms build digital capabilities to improve their environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance while addressing challenges in integrating digital solutions for sustainability.

The collection recognizes that entrepreneurial ventures, characterized by innovation and agility, play a critical role in advancing digital-driven sustainable business practices. Improved ESG performance is essential for managing environmental and social risks, enhancing corporate reputation, and meeting stakeholder expectations regarding ethical and responsible business conduct. The collection welcomes experimental, conceptual, theoretical, and empirical studies that examine the intersection of digital capabilities and ESG performance in entrepreneurial firms, illuminate obstacles, and propose practical solutions.

Appel publié par International Entrepreneurship and Management Journal. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How do entrepreneurial ventures define and measure ESG performance in the digital era? What critical digital capabilities contribute to their improved ESG performance?
  • What challenges do entrepreneurial firms face in integrating digital solutions to enhance environmental sustainability? What could be the best practices for tackling those challenges?
  • What are the possible learning mechanisms and knowledge-sharing processes within entrepreneurial ecosystems that could foster development of digital capabilities for ESG goals?
  • What roles do leadership and organizational culture play in fostering digital capabilities for superior ESG performance in entrepreneurial firms?
  • How can entrepreneurial firms effectively utilize digital technologies to measure and improve their environmental performance within ESG frameworks?
  • How can digital capabilities be harnessed to address diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) challenges in entrepreneurial firms, contributing to improved social sustainability?
  • How do digitalization efforts impact the governance structures of entrepreneurial firms in the context of sustainability? What actions could be taken to improve it?
  • To what extent do regulatory frameworks influence the adoption of digital strategies for ESG compliance in entrepreneurial settings?
  • How do digital technologies facilitate transparency and accountability in ESG reporting for entrepreneurial firms?
  • How can entrepreneurial firms balance profitability goals with sustainable practices through digital transformations? Under this scenario, which opportunities and challenges could arise?
  • What lessons can we learn from recent, real-world cases that showcase the impact of digital capabilities on ESG performance in different industries, particularly entrepreneurial firms, and how can new guidelines lead toward improved ESG performance?

item.title: Digitalization for responsive and circular supply chains
item.content:encoded:
Günter Prockl, Copenhagen Business School

Alexander Pflaum, University of Bamberg

Haozhe Chen, Iowa State University

Marcel Papert, University of Bamberg

Modern supply chains face unprecedented disruptions while simultaneously confronting environmental limits and resource scarcity. This requires a fundamental transformation toward more responsive and circular systems. Digital technologies including IoT, AI, digital twins, and blockchain are critical enablers for building resilient supply chains that adapt quickly to change while reducing resource consumption and closing material loops.

The special issue seeks papers demonstrating how digital and data-driven solutions implement these responsive and circular supply chains, along with their associated business models. Contributions should explore digital technologies across multiple supply chain tiers, with particular emphasis on industry-specific applications and the integration of responsiveness, servitization, and sustainability goals.

item.title: Sustainable Maritime Transportation: New Insights from Artificial Intelligence
item.content:encoded:
This special issue focuses on the intersection of sustainable maritime transportation and artificial intelligence technologies. Maritime transportation plays a crucial role in global commerce and logistics, accounting for a significant portion of international trade. However, the shipping industry faces considerable environmental challenges, including greenhouse gas emissions, fuel consumption, and pollution. Artificial intelligence and machine learning offer promising opportunities to address these sustainability challenges while improving operational efficiency.

The special issue welcomes contributions that explore innovative AI-based solutions for enhancing sustainability in maritime transportation. This includes research on optimizing vessel performance, reducing carbon footprints, improving safety protocols, and developing intelligent systems for port and logistics management. We are particularly interested in studies that demonstrate practical applications of AI technologies in real-world maritime contexts.

item.title: A Decade (2015-2025) of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): Trends, Reflections, and Realignments in Hospitality and Tourism Research
item.content:encoded:
Edmund Goh, Les Roches Abu Dhabi Hospitality Academy

Jun Wen, Macau University of Science and Technology

Siamak Seyfi, University of Oulu

C. Michael Hall, Massey University

Xin-Jean Lim, Sun Yat-Sen University

September 2025 marked the 10th anniversary of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), a global blueprint for achieving peace, prosperity, and planetary wellbeing. Over the past decade, the hospitality and tourism industries and destination communities have emerged as powerful platforms for advancing and contesting these goals. Hospitality and tourism encompass all 17 SDGs, either directly or indirectly, from economic growth and decent work (SDG 8) to responsible consumption and production (SDG 12), climate action (SDG 13), and partnerships for the goals (SDG 17).

Appel publié par Current Issues in Tourism. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Reflecting on the First Decade (2015–2025) of SDG achievements and gaps
  • Critical reviews of how research to date references SDGs and where conceptual or methodological gaps persist
  • Evaluating tourism and hospitality's contribution to all 17 SDGs, including SDG 1 (No Poverty) and SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) through community tourism, local sourcing, and food redistribution
  • Examining progress toward SDG 3 (Good Health and Wellbeing) through wellness tourism, workplace health initiatives, and traveller safety
  • Assessing SDG 4 (Quality Education) via tourism and hospitality curriculum transformation, sustainability literacy, and lifelong learning
  • Policy coherence and alignment of tourism strategies with SDG 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions), focusing on governance, transparency, and ethical practices
  • Reviewing the role of SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure) in sustainable destination design, transport systems, and smart tourism
  • Integrating SDG 8 (Decent Work), SDG 5 (Gender Equality), and SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities) through inclusive recruitment, fair wages, and leadership opportunities
  • Advancing SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production) via food waste management, circular hospitality systems, and sustainable event management

item.title: Innovations in Production Planning: Emerging Problems and Modern Solution Paradigms
item.content:encoded:

Production planning has historically been a central pillar of industrial engineering and operations management. Since the mid-20th century, the field has developed a rich body of classical problems and models, such as lot sizing, job shop and flow shop scheduling, capacity planning, assembly line balancing, material requirements planning (MRP), and aggregate production planning. These models provided structured ways to allocate resources, balance supply and demand, and coordinate activities across production systems, often under deterministic assumptions and with objectives focused primarily on cost and efficiency. Linear programming, dynamic programming, and combinatorial optimization offered rigorous formulations and exact methods, while heuristics and metaheuristics emerged to address large-scale and computationally complex instances.

Driven by the deep integration of digital economy, intelligent manufacturing and modern logistics industry, low-altitude airspace resources have gradually become a key new carrier for breaking through the bottlenecks of traditional ground logistics. Low-altitude logistics, which is enabled by drones, unmanned aerial vehicles, intelligent terminals, digital platforms and low-altitude airspace management, has been emerging as a new frontier in logistics and supply chain management. Unlike traditional logistics systems that mainly rely on ground-based transportation, warehousing and distribution networks, it extends logistics operations into three-dimensional, air-ground integrated systems. item.content:encoded:

Food and beverage advertising has long emphasized nourishment, affordability, and convenience. Yet this perspective no longer captures contemporary consumption trends or the complex role of advertising. Many consumers adopt dietary regimes—even without medical necessity—as expressions of identity and self-esteem. Advertising reflects this shift by positioning consumption of "healthier" options such as gluten-free snacks, keto-friendly products, vegan substitutes, or diet beverages as lifestyle choices tied to self-image. Campaigns for plant-based milk, for example, highlight wellness and modernity, appealing to aspirational goals beyond nutrition. Beyond individual identity, advertising also conveys cultural and social values: halal- and kosher-certified products underscore cultural continuity, while fine wines, gourmet chocolates, and craft spirits are framed as markers of refinement and status. Increasingly, campaigns link food to place-based identity, such as agritourism promotions that emphasize heritage, authenticity, and local cuisine.

item.title: Alternative Proteins for Sustainable and Ethical Food Systems: Consumer, Production, and Supply-Chain Perspectives
item.content:encoded:
The global food system is undergoing profound transformation driven by growing concerns about climate change, biodiversity loss, animal welfare, public health, and the long-term sustainability of livestock-based production models. Against this backdrop, alternative proteins, including cultured meat, plant-based meat analogues, insect-based products and novel dairy substitutes, have emerged as promising pathways for addressing environmental pressures while meeting evolving consumer expectations for ethical, healthy and sustainable diets. Although consumer research on these products has expanded rapidly, a comprehensive understanding of how alternative proteins reshape the broader agrifood system remains limited. Existing studies often address consumption, production, regulation, and socio-cultural dynamics in isolation, leaving significant knowledge gaps regarding value-chain restructuring, producer adoption, economic feasibility, and governance.

While many of these countries are rapidly industrializing and increasingly integrated into global value chains, they often lack the regulatory infrastructures, institutional capacity, and enforcement mechanisms necessary to ensure environmentally responsible economic activity. item.content:encoded:
This special issue aims to advance scholarly knowledge on how multinational enterprises (MNEs) form international partnerships to create social value. Research in multinational business scholarship has examined the international activities of MNEs in addressing the broader sustainability agenda. However, there remains limited understanding of the specific challenges, tensions, and opportunities MNEs face when engaging in multi-stakeholder international partnerships for social value creation. Given the increasing centrality of such partnerships in global sustainability efforts, addressing this gap is both timely and important. The motivation for this special issue is to advance new theoretical and empirical knowledge into how MNEs' international partnerships enable social value creation.

item.title: Multinational enterprises, sustainability and innovation in the digital age: Global, regional and local perspectives
item.content:encoded:
Achieving net-zero targets poses significant challenges for economies, governments, and societies worldwide. Multinational enterprises (MNEs) are central actors in this transition, both as developers and adopters of renewable energy and low-carbon technologies. As primary boundary spanners, they manage global value chains and partnerships across diverse institutional contexts and consumer markets. MNEs increasingly navigate a complex landscape of incentives, sanctions, and regulatory barriers that vary by sector, technology platform, country, and region. Politically motivated disruptions—including shifting tariff and non-tariff barriers and uneven low-carbon policies—compound these challenges, placing premium value on managerial capabilities.

Two emerging developments motivate this Special Issue. First, digital technologies offer new potential to enhance firm-level capabilities for coordinating and adapting cross-border networks, while reshaping competitive dynamics between incumbents, startups, and scale-ups. Second, China's ascendancy as both innovator and regulator—particularly in new energy technologies—and its growing geopolitical influence demand renewed scholarly attention.

item.title: Reimagining Sustainable Future and Managing Change
item.content:encoded:
Many unprecedented developments over the past few years, such as geopolitical shocks, social upheavals, uncertainty over new technologies like AI, recurring natural disasters, and sustained uncertainty about climate change, have forced a rethink of a sustainable future. While parameters of change and transformations are themselves undergoing drastic changes in ways that were never expected, day-to-day survival strategies take precedence. As a result, there is growing concern about whether societies, organisations, communities and individuals can continue with the existing notions of a sustainable future.

New debates and discourses have kindled the need for reimagining ideas and perspectives of a sustainable future world. These discussions span a large domain of ideas, including organisational strategy formulation, stakeholder management, supply chain reconfiguration, organisational development, etc. Emerging literature signposts tough decisions, organisational anxieties, change management barriers, and possible solutions as organisations confront difficult and unprecedented organisational transformations.

item.title: Social Marketing and Sustainable Futures
item.content:encoded:
Social marketing has long been positioned as a discipline capable of improving societal wellbeing by applying marketing principles to influence behaviour in socially beneficial ways. Early contributions that imagined marketing being used beyond the commercial realm laid the foundation for the field's formal emergence in the early 1970s. Over the decades, social marketing has advanced its understanding of how to encourage and sustain behaviour change, yet the contemporary landscape presents challenges of a fundamentally different scale.

Increasing environmental degradation, climate instability, resource pressures, and persistent social inequities highlight the need for social marketing approaches capable of addressing system-wide issues. While behaviour remains a central concern, scholars have argued that meaningful progress requires attention to macro-level structures and the dynamic interactions among actors, networks, institutions, and infrastructures. Social marketing is therefore being called upon not merely to promote individual behaviour change, but to support the creation of sustainable futures through coordinated, multi-level forms of change.

item.title: Transforming Management Accounting: Digitalisation, Sustainability and Organisational Change
item.content:encoded:
Umesh Sharma, University of Waikato

Chris Akroyd, University of Waikato

Yuki Guo, University of Auckland

Leanne Johnstone, Orebro University School of Business

This special issue seeks to advance understanding of how management accounting is evolving in response to digitalisation, sustainability challenges, and ongoing organisational transformation. In recent years, rapid technological developments—including data analytics, artificial intelligence, and digital platforms—have fundamentally reshaped organisational information systems and decision-making processes. At the same time, organisations face increasing pressure to respond to climate change, environmental degradation, and broader socio-economic challenges. These developments are redefining expectations of management accounting, extending its role beyond traditional financial control toward supporting sustainable value creation and long-term organisational resilience.

item.title: Well-Being in B2B Marketing: Rethinking B2B Marketing for a New Era
item.content:encoded:
This special issue advances interdisciplinary understanding of well-being in B2B marketing. It examines how well-being reshapes value creation, inter-organizational relationships, and sustainable business practices. Despite growing interest in individual-level well-being (e.g., salesperson burnout), B2B marketing lacks integrative frameworks examining well-being across inter-organizational networks. The special issue aims to develop a holistic and sustainability-oriented perspective on well-being within B2B markets.
